author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.

slides.1: Good morning. Is school in Taiwan fair for every child? Today we look at SDG 4, Quality Education. On paper we look great, but science class tells a different story.
slides.2: What does SDG 4 promise? Education for everyone, rich or poor, at any age. Taiwan builds computer chips for the world. But do our schools teach us to use them wisely?
slides.3: Taiwan puts big money into science and math, and that is how we grew rich. But our birth rate has never been lower. Are we spending on the right problems?
slides.4: Here is the first problem. In 1990 Taiwan had more than 300,000 babies. Last year we had fewer than 140,000. In the countryside, schools close and children travel far.
slides.5: Next, think about exams. In science class students learn facts by heart, but they rarely ask their own questions. Many drop science early, so can that fix climate change?
slides.6: Money is not shared evenly. A city classroom has new labs and tablets, while a village school waits. Surveys put the equipment gap near 30%, so who will fix it?
slides.7: Now the good news. Education here is free for 12 years, and 99% of children finish primary school. That matches the best in the OECD. But is the teaching any good?
slides.8: The government also pays for preschool. Today 96% of poorer five-year-olds go to class. They learn to count, to ask and to share. That helps them in science later.
slides.9: More people here finish high school and college than almost anywhere. Our teachers also train hard. But do all towns teach science at the same depth?
slides.10: So what are we doing about it? The government now pays for hands-on science. Students build things instead of only reading. They start coding, and they ask when AI is fair.
slides.11: More than 80% of our schools now use tablets and apps. Classes run experiments on a screen. That links them to our chip factories, but we must also teach honest use.
slides.12: Some students join a special program and spend time inside tech firms. They meet green energy engineers. A school topic slowly turns into a real job.
slides.13: Why does this matter? Taiwan sells about 500 billion dollars of goods a year, and technology is most of it. The same science helps us plan for flooding and heat.
slides.14: But look around the engineering class. Only 30% of the students are women. Many people still say that science is for boys, and that thinking belongs in the past.
slides.15: If we leave these gaps open, we will waste bright young people. Ask your own teachers a simple question. Is this college ready for the jobs that AI is creating?
slides.16: Good schools make a country strong. If we change nothing, Taiwan will slowly fall behind. Our science lessons have to grow with the world, because tomorrow will not wait.
slides.17: So where does that leave us? Taiwan has built a wide, free education system, and STEM has made the country rich. Yet fairness is still the missing piece.
slides.18: High test scores are not enough. A score cannot show me a creative idea, and it cannot make a poor school rich. We have to rebuild the system, not decorate it.
slides.19: In the future, science must open its doors wider. Girls, country students and poorer families belong in the lab. Every lesson should show where the science lands in real life.
slides.20: Here is my ask. Join a school meeting, help a younger classmate, or speak up for a fairer rule. Together, Taiwan can build a school that misses nobody. Let's start today.
